notes.text: And — And having said that the Assyrian yoke should be destroyed because of the anointing, he now explains who that anointed person was. The stem - Or, stump: for the word signifies properly a trunk cut off from the root. By which he clearly implies, that the Messiah should be born of the royal house of David, at that time when it was in a most forlorn condition, like a tree cut down, and whereof nothing is left but a stump or root under ground. Of Jesse - He doth not say of David, but of Jesse, who was a private and mean person, to intimate, that at the time of Christ's birth the royal family should be reduced to its primitive obscurity.

Wisdom — It is not needful, exactly to distinguish these two gifts; it is sufficient that they are necessary qualifications for a governor, and a teacher, and it is evident they signify perfect knowledge of all things necessary for his own and peoples good, and a sound judgment, to distinguish between things that differ. Counsel - Of prudence, to give good counsel; and of might and courage, to execute it. Knowledge - Of the perfect knowledge of the whole will and counsel of God, as also of all secret things, yea of the hearts of men. Fear - A fear of reverence, a care to please him, and lothness to offend him.

In the fear — He shall not judge rashly and partially, but considerately and justly, as the fear of God obliges all Judges to do. Judge - Of persons or causes. After the sight - According to outward appearance, as men do, because they cannot search mens hearts. Reprove - Condemn or pass sentence against a person. His ears - By uncertain rumours or suggestions.

Judge — Defend and deliver them. Reprove - Or condemn their malicious enemies. Thy rod - With his word, which is his scepter, and the rod of his power, Psalm cx, 2, which is sharper than a sword, Heb. iv, 12, by the preaching whereof he subdued the world to himself, and will destroy his enemies, 2Thes ii, 8. This he adds farther, to declare the nature of Christ's kingdom, that it is not of this world.

The girdle — It shall adorn him, and be the glory of his government, as a girdle was used for an ornament, chap. iii, 24, and as an ensign of power, Job xii, 18, and it shall constantly cleave to him in all his administrations, as a girdle cleaveth to a man's loins.

The wolf — The creatures shall be restored to that state of innocency in which they were before the fall of man. Men of fierce, and cruel dispositions, shall be so transformed by the grace of Christ, that they shall become gentle, and tractable. A child - They will submit their rebellious wills to the conduct of the meanest persons that speak to them in Christ's name.
Feed — Together, without any danger or fear. Straw - The grass of the earth, as they did at first, and shall not devour other living creatures.
My holy mountain — In Zion, in my church. The sea - The channel of the sea.

A root — A branch growing upon the root. Ensign - Shall grow up into a great tree, shall become an eminent ensign. The people - Which not only the Jews, but all nations, may discern, and to which they shall resort. Rest - His resting-place, his temple or church, the place of his presence and abode. Glorious - Shall be filled with greater glory than the Jewish tabernacle and temple were; only this glory shall be spiritual, consisting in the plentiful effusions of the gifts, and graces, of the Holy Spirit.

glossa.text:
*And there shall come forth a rod.* ((HIER.)) Up to the beginning of the vision of Babylon the prophecy is of Christ, which we expound by parts, lest we confound the memory of the reader.

*Shall come forth.* The Jews interpret the rod and the flower to be Christ himself, etc., *as far as* and thou art my firstborn Son, who reignest for ever.

*And shall rest.* ((ID.)) Because in him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead.

*The Spirit.* As the word of the Lord is called light, life and resurrection, etc., *as far as* these are the seven eyes upon one stone, according to Zacharias.

*And the spirit shall fill him.* ((ID.)) Spiritually, for the sake of the little ones who have need of fear, which perfect charity casts out. For he that fears has punishment, and is not perfect in charity.

*Not according to.* He shall not accept the person, because God is not an accepter of persons, but in every nation he that fears God is acceptable to him.

*He shall reprove.* ((ID.)) The Pharisees, and them that reproved the apostles *apotolos*, when, walking on the sabbath through the corn, they plucked the ears with their hands and rubbed them and ate.

*The rod of his mouth.* ((ID.)) By the rod the sentence of judgment can be understood. For in the beginning of his preaching he said: *Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven shall draw near;* and he subjoined: *Every tree that doth not bring forth good fruits shall be rooted up and cast into the fire.*

*He shall slay the wicked one.* For if Michael shall slay him (as some say), yet God himself shall do this in Michael.

*Faith.* ((HIER.)) The faithful, by working well, shall cleave to him who was made wisdom, justice and sanctification, who says: *I am light and life.*

*The wolf with the lamb.* ((ID.)) Paul with Peter, whence: *Benjamin a ravening wolf.* And: *Feed my sheep. The wolf shall dwell with the lamb.* It was not the lamb and the kid that dwelt with the wolf and the leopard, but the wolf and the leopard imitate the innocence of the lambs and the kids, namely Christ.

*The wolf shall dwell.* ((HIER.)) Our judaizing Jews, etc., *as far as* nothing evil, save baseness.

((ID.)) The calf and the sheep, the humble and the innocent, etc., *as far as* let the Church furnish this in the world.

*The lion as the ox,* etc. ((ID.)) For the princes of this world, and other simple folk, are content with the surface of the history; for they do not understand the wheat and the marrow, that is, the inner sense.

*The infant.* Christ, or the apostles, children in malice, perfect in understanding: who cast out demons from possessed bodies.

*Of the basilisk.* The basilisk, the king of all serpents, etc., *as far as* from possessed bodies, namely.

 *The hand.* That is, the divine power: he shall deliver up captive the asp or the basilisk thereupon seized, that is, the devil.
*For it is filled.* After his manner, at the end the prophetic words are laid open, lest they be taken to the letter.

*Who standeth for a sign,* whence: *Behold this child is set for the ruin and for the resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be contradicted ((Luc. II))*. The Seventy: Who shall rise up to be a prince, etc., *as far as* the same signifies a sepulchre. For a sleeping and a rest, with another word but the same sense, we have rendered *sepulchre.*

notes.text: Judgments — He saith judgments in the plural number, because though the office of judging and ruling was but one, yet there were divers parts and branches, of it; in all which he begs that Solomon may be directed to do as God would have him to do.
Thy afflicted ones — For such are thine in a special manner, thou art their judge and patron.
The mountains — Which are so dangerous to passengers, in regard of robbers and wild beasts. Hereby it is implied, that other places should do so too, and that it should be common and universal.
Judge — Vindicate them from their oppressors.

Thee — Thee, O God, this shall be another blessed fruit of this righteous government, that together with peace, true religion shall be established, and that throughout all generations, which was begun in Solomon's days, but not fully accomplished 'till Christ came.
He shall come — Christ did come down from heaven, and brought or sent down from heaven his doctrine, (which is often compared to rain) and the sweet and powerful influences of his spirit.

glossa.text: *Unto Solomon,* etc. ((AUG.)) The true peaceable one, etc., *as far as* he who is here commended according to each nature. ((CAS.)) The fourth psalm concerning the two natures of Christ admonishes that we should believe Christ, true God and true man, to be king, and it is a prophecy about Christ.

*O God, judgment.* ((CAS.)) Concerning the judgment, in wishing that it be given to the Son. *Thy justice,* etc. ((AUG.)) Note that repetitions of the same thing, or in other words, greatly commend the divine utterances, which are chiefly in the psalms: and in that kind of speech by which the affection of the mind is to be moved.

*Mountains.* ((AUG.)) The Prophets, the Apostles, who by their height come near to heaven; *peace* to be announced to the faithful people, Christ. *And the hills.* Let them receive *justice,* that is, Christ, or *the mountains peace for the people:* and *hills* he says of both sorts of preachers, those going before and those following. Or *let the mountains receive,* that is, the greater ones.

*Peace.* The word of reconciliation, namely the word of the Gospel, to this end, that they may announce it to the people.

*And the hills.* That is, the lesser ones; justice, that is, obedience, that they may obey the teaching of truth.

By saying *thine* and *thy own,* he shows that all things which are the Father's are the Son's also, and conversely.

*He shall judge the poor of the people.* ((CAS.)) He treats the same matter concerning the same judgment, by affirming it. After the wish, by the power of prophecy, he says what things are to be furnished at the Lord's coming. ((AUG.)) Or according to another reading: *Justice shall judge the poor man.* But those codices which have [it] in the letter are the more approved. *The poor of the people.* That is, those who are poor among the people, in which the good and the bad are mingled together. *He shall humble the calumniator.* For while he helps by his grace, etc., *as far as* he who strives to drag the innocent into guilt. ((HIERON., AUG.)) Or, *he shall humble,* and, the devil being conquered, *there shall remain with the sun* a brightness; that is, the Son with the Father, sitting at the Father's right hand for ever, that is *before the moon,* unto generation and generation.

*He shall come down like rain,* etc. ((CAS.)) Behold who and of what sort is that king who is to judge. ((AUG.)) He alludes to the deed of Gedeon, etc., *as far as* and afterwards the Gentile world was rained upon, the fleece of the Jews being dry. ((CAS.)) Christ shall come down, etc., *as far as* who then, after such open likenesses, doubts of the Virgin's childbearing? *Into the fleece, and like drops.* ((AUG.)) *The fleece,* Judaea, which was to be despoiled of the authority of doctrine, as a sheep of its fleece: or, because it withheld the rain of doctrine, which it was unwilling to preach to the Gentiles.

notes.text: Aforetime — In the Old Testament. That we through patience and consolation of the scriptures may have hope - That through the consolation which God gives us by these, we may have patience and a joyful hope.
According to the power of Christ Jesus.
That ye — Both Jews and gentiles, believing with one mind, and confessing with one mouth.
Receive ye one another — Weak and strong, with mutual love.

Now I say — The apostle here shows how Christ received us. Christ Jesus-Jesus is the name, Christ the surname. The latter was first known to the Jews; the former, to the gentiles. Therefore he is styled Jesus Christ, when the words stand in the common, natural order. When the order is inverted, as here, the office of Christ is more solemnly considered. Was a servant - Of his Father. Of the circumcision - For the salvation of the circumcised, the Jews. For the truth of God - To manifest the truth and fidelity of God.
As it is written — In the eighteenth Psalm, here the gentiles and Jews are spoken of as joining in the worship of the God of Israel. Psalm xviii, 49
Deut. xxxii, 43.
Psalm cxvii, 1.

There shall be the root of Jesse — That kings and the Messiah should spring from his house, was promised to Jesse before it was to David. In him shall the gentiles hope - Who before had been "without hope," Eph. ii, 12. Isaiah xi, 10

Now the God of hope — A glorious title of God, but till now unknown to the heathens; for their goddess Hope, like their other idols, was nothing; whose temple at Rome was burned by lightning. It was, indeed, built again not long after, but was again burned to the ground.

glossa.text: *To be of one mind.* As if he should say: Unless ye be of the same mind, ye will not be able to honor God.

*Of the circumcision.* That is, of the Jews, to whom he came bodily; whence: *I am not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel ((Matth. XV))*. *For the truth.* He did not cast off the Jews, to whom truth belongs properly, and mercy to the gentiles, to whom no promise had been made. *The promises.* For he had promised to Abraham: *In thy seed shall all nations be blessed ((Gen. XXII))*. And to David: *Of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne ((Psalm. CXXXI))*. And likewise Jacob said: *There shall rise a star out of Jacob ((Num. XXIV))*.
*I will confess.* But confession is not only of sins, but also of praise.

*There shall be a root of Jesse.* And of this root shall be he that shall rise up, etc. Jesse is the root, David the tree, which by the branch, that is, Mary, brought forth the fruit, that is, Christ.

*And with peace.* That ye may be able to rejoice, may he give peace and concord toward one another; and this will be, if the faith be sound. *That ye may abound.* That is, that by having these things ye may be the more certain of eternal blessedness, and may abound in the virtue of the Holy Ghost, that is, in the fortitude of good working, which is given through the Holy Ghost.

notes.text: In those days — that is, while Jesus dwelt there. In the wilderness of Judea - This was a wilderness properly so called, a wild, barren, desolate place as was that also where our Lord was tempted. But, generally speaking, a wilderness in the New Testament means only a common, or less cultivated place, in opposition to pasture and arable land. Mark i, 1; Luke iii, 1.

The kingdom of heaven, and the kingdom of God, are but two phrases for the same thing. They mean, not barely a future happy state, in heaven, but a state to be enjoyed on earth: the proper disposition for the glory of heaven, rather than the possession of it. Is at hand — As if he had said, God is about to erect that kingdom, spoken of by Daniel, Dan. ii, 44; vii, 13, 14; the kingdom of the God of heaven. It properly signifies here, the Gospel dispensation, in which subjects were to be gathered to God by his Son, and a society to be formed, which was to subsist first on earth, and afterward with God in glory. In some places of Scripture, the phrase more particularly denotes the state of it on earth: in, others, it signifies only the state of glory: but it generally includes both. The Jews understood it of a temporal kingdom, the seat of which they supposed would be Jerusalem; and the expected sovereign of this kingdom they learned from Daniel to call the Son of man. Both John the Baptist and Christ took up that phrase, the kingdom of heaven, as they found it, and gradually taught the Jews (though greatly unwilling to learn) to understand it right. The very demand of repentance, as previous to it, showed it was a spiritual kingdom, and that no wicked man, how politic, brave, or learned soever, could possibly be a subject of it.
The way of the Lord — Of Christ. Make his paths straight - By removing every thing which might prove a hindrance to his gracious appearance. Isaiah xl, 3.

John had his raiment of camel's hair — Coarse and rough, suiting his character and doctrine. A leathern girdle - Like Elijah, in whose spirit and power he came. His food was locusts and wild honey - Locusts are ranked among clean meats, Lev. xi, 22. But these were not always to be had. So in default of those, he fed on wild honey.

Confessing their sins — Of their own accord; freely and openly. Such prodigious numbers could hardly be baptized by immerging their whole bodies under water: nor can we think they were provided with change of raiment for it, which was scarcely practicable for such vast multitudes. And yet they could not be immerged naked with modesty, nor in their wearing apparel with safety. It seems, therefore, that they stood in ranks on the edge of the river, and that John, passing along before them, cast water on their heads or faces, by which means he might baptize many thousands in a day. And this way most naturally signified Christ's baptizing them with the Holy Ghost and with fire, which John spoke of, as prefigured by his baptizing with water, and which was eminently fulfilled, when the Holy Ghost sat upon the disciples in the appearance of tongues, or flames of fire.

The Pharisees were a very ancient sect among the Jews. They took their name from a Hebrew word, which signifies to separate, because they separated themselves from all other men. They were outwardly strict observers of the law, fasted often, made long prayers, rigorously kept the Sabbath, and paid all tithe, even of mint, anise, and cummin. Hence they were in high esteem among the people. But inwardly, they were full of pride and hypocrisy. The Sadducees were another sect among the Jews, only not so considerable as the Pharisees. They denied the existence of angels, and the immortality of the soul, and by consequence the resurrection of the dead. Ye brood of vipers — In like manner, the crafty Herod is styled a fox, and persons of insidious, ravenous, profane, or sensual dispositions, are named respectively by him who saw their hearts, serpents, dogs, wolves, and swine; terms which are not the random language of passion, but a judicious designation of the persons meant by them. For it was fitting such men should be marked out, either for a caution to others, or a warning to themselves.

Repentance is of two sorts; that which is termed legal, and that which is styled evangelical repentance. The former (which is the same that is spoken of here) is a thorough conviction of sin. The latter is a change of heart (and consequently of life) from all sin to all holiness.

And say not confidently — The word in the original, vulgarly rendered, Think not, seems here, and in many places, not to diminish, but rather add to the force of the word with which it is joined. We have Abraham to our father - It is almost incredible, how great the presumption of the Jews was on this their relation to Abraham. One of their famous sayings was, "Abraham sits near the gates of hell, and suffers no Israelite to go down into it." I say unto you - This preface always denotes the importance of what follows. Of these stones - Probably pointing to those which lay before them.

But the axe also already lieth — That is, there is no room for such idle pretenses. Speedy execution is determined against all that do not repent. The comparison seems to be taken from a woodman that has laid down his axe to put off his coat, and then immediately goes to work to cut down the tree. This refers to the wrath to come in verse 7. Is hewn down - Instantly, without farther delay.

He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire — He shall fill you with the Holy Ghost, inflaming your hearts with that fire of love, which many waters cannot quench. And this was done, even with a visible appearance as of fire, on the day of pentecost.

Whose fan — That is, the word of the Gospel. His floor - That is, his Church, which is now covered with a mixture of wheat and chaff. He will gather the wheat into the garner - Will lay up those who are truly good in heaven.

glossa.text: *In those days.* He passes over many things, and crosses to the preaching of John. *In those days.* He takes in not the years of boyhood only, but all of them up to the preaching of John, that is, when he was nearly thirty years old. Luke expresses the times more exactly: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. *Preaching.* He who had before kept silence made himself known by baptizing, preparing the way for the Lord. *In the desert of Judaea.* Because the Jews had been deserted by God, and for them repentance is necessary, that they may return.

*Repentance.* The herald announces this, which afterwards the Truth announces through himself; repentance goes before, the promise of the kingdom follows: he who truly repents, in himself his past errors, then lifts up his mind to the heavenly kingdom. If remission is made freely in baptism, why is repentance preached? But the manner of repentance is threefold. The first, to renounce and condemn errors and all evils before baptism: which is necessary for those who are coming to Christ. The second, that those who have fallen after baptism be called back through repentance. The third, whereby the saints are daily cleansed of such sins as life is not lived without.

To repent is to weep for things done before, and not to commit what must be wept for. The kingdom of heaven is said to be at hand for the penitent. Not earthly things, as in the old law: and this through the obedience of Christ. And John first preached this kingdom of heaven: *Do penance.* The first virtue is, through repentance to slay the old man, and to hate vices: and he who does not do this not only fails to lay hold of the virtues, but does not even escape punishments. The virtue of repentance is conceived by fear, which is the beginning of wisdom. Repentance is from punishing, whereby each man punishes what he has unlawfully committed.

To do penance is to make fruits worthy of repentance. *The kingdom of heaven.* That is, Christ, through whom the saints reign in the heavenly places. Or the Gospel, by which he invites to the kingdom.

 *For it hath drawn near,* etc. Unless it had drawn near, no one could return: because the weak and the blind were without the way (which is Christ): and John, preparing that way, sets it before the penitent.

*The voice of one crying.* John is the voice, Christ the word, who cries in John: No word is heard without a voice, nor is a voice of any avail without the understanding of the word. The voice prepares the way for the word, that it may be received. Whence: *I have prepared a lamp for my Christ ((Psal. CXXXI))*.

*In the desert.* A pattern for the penitent: the place of his converse is not the throng of men, but the desert. His clothing is not soft to the point of looseness, but rough: his food scanty and unaccustomed.

Typically, the desert signifies the life of the saints, set apart from the enticements of the world.

 *The way of the Lord.* The way of the Lord is made straight to the heart, when his word is diligently heard.

*And John himself.* He who preaches repentance displays the habit of repentance. In him the meanness of clothing and of food is praised, the use of which in the rich man is called to account.

And John himself instructs the penitent in his own person, and sets forth a pattern of life by dwelling in the desert, living on locusts, clothing himself in camel's hair.

The servant of God ought not to have clothing for adornment or for delight, but only for covering nakedness. Hence John was clothed in hair.

*Then there went out to him,* etc. Because unless a man go out from evils, he is not washed. Whence it fitly follows: *They were baptized by him in the Jordan:* which is interpreted *a going down*, because they were going down from the pride of the old man to the humility of confession and amendment. For already then an example was given to those about to be baptized, of confessing sins and promising better things.

*In the Jordan.* Because in it the figure of baptism went before, and from its name it requires a going down from pride, which is fitting for the baptized. *Confessing.* The confession of sins is the testimony of a conscience that fears God. For he who fears the judgment of God is not ashamed to confess his sins. More perfectly, fear looses every shame. The confession of sin has shame in it, and that blushing is itself a heavy punishment. And therefore we are bidden to confess our sins, that we may suffer the blushing for a punishment. For this very thing is part of the divine judgment.

*Many of the Pharisees,* etc. These are of the heretics of the Jews, and the Pharisees set the righteousness of observances and traditions before all else. Whence also they are called Pharisees, that is, divided from the people by a private righteousness. The Sadducees, that is, the just: for they claim for themselves what they are not: these deny the resurrection, saying that the soul perishes with the body: they receive the five books of Moses, they reject the prophets. These, when they come to baptism, John rebukes: because they most of all had need of correction and repentance.

*Brood of vipers,* etc., that is, poisoned sons of the poisoned: because they envy the good and persecute them, they wound their neighbors as their fathers did.

The viper kills its own father, so the Jews killed the prophets who were their fathers.

*Bring forth therefore fruits worthy. ((BEDA.))* As if he were saying: Why do you not first lay aside your poisons, that so to baptism, etc., *as far as* it is grace that feels, and feeling seeks holiness.

*For I say.* He draws them back from the flesh, that they may consider the works of God's predestination. The first are the rudiments of faith, to believe that God can do whatever he will, so that he who created all things out of nothing can form sons of Abraham from stones or from dust. *Of stones.* Pointing to those stones which Josue caused to be carried over out of the Jordan, toward which he says this as though stretching out his finger.

Josue caused twelve stones to be carried from the midst of the Jordan onto dry land, and others to be set in their place out of the land in the same channel: by which the blinding of the Jews and the transforming of the Gentiles to the light are foresignified.

Or he calls the Gentiles stones: and the sense is: Do not glory in the seed of the flesh: because these only are the sons of God who have been enlightened by grace and inwardly raised up. He says "raise up" pointedly, because Christ received Sara, that is, the Church, and raises up sons of Abraham by grace, he having died without children, lest so great a patriarch should be deprived of the promises. In presage of this thing God once begot a son of Sara.

*For now the axe.* But lest they should seem free of danger if they kept themselves apart from such sacraments, he threatens. *The axe.* Christ, who consists of haft and iron, that is, of the humanity by which he is held, and the divinity because he cuts. *Is laid:* because although he waits through patience, he yet sees what he is about to do. *To the root.* That is, the end of the Jewish people, that he may take away from the land of the living those who do not believe in Christ. Or, the axe is the sentence of judgment, or the preaching of the Gospel. *To the root.* Note, not to the branches, but to the root. For when the sons of the wicked are taken away, what else is cut off but the branches of an unfruitful tree? When the whole offspring is taken away together with the parent, the tree is cut off at the root, that nothing may remain from which some shoot might spring up again. The roots are thoughts, by which men, being planted, are either lifted up on high to heaven, or sent down to the depths of hell. The tree is the human race: of this tree some branches are dry, that is, the pagans, fit for the burning. Others are green, but without fruit: as the hypocrites, who make a show of holiness, but are empty within: others are fruitful, but poisonous, that is, the heretics: who by preaching bring forth fruit, but a deadly fruit. Others, that is, the catholics, who bear good fruit. *Every tree therefore,* as the Gentiles, the hypocrites, who bear none, and the heretics, who bear evil fruit.

*I indeed.* Lest he should seem to threaten on his own authority, he begins to disclose of how great dignity he is: whose presence he holds out as a threat, or whose benefit he urges upon them: *I indeed baptize you in water.* I only wash bodies, because I cannot loose sins, so that as I run before in being born and in preaching, so I do in baptizing: that I may direct to the baptism of Christ the penitent, whom I mark off by this sign from the impenitent. *He who is to come after me.* And though I admonish you to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance, to cast away pride: yet I cannot loose from sins. *He is mightier than I.* Because I baptize unto repentance, he unto remission. I have the Spirit, he gives it. I preach the kingdom of heaven, he gives it.

*Whose I am not,* etc. Others write: Whose I am not worthy to loose the latchet of his shoe. Now John could have said both, either in one continuous speech or at different times: so that one evangelist took up this, another that. Yet all of them told the truth. His aim in this is to show the excellence of Christ and his own humility.

Or according to the allegory. The shoe is the mystery of the incarnation; the latchet, the tying of the mystery. Therefore John is not able to loose the latchet, because he does not suffice to search out the mystery of the incarnation. Or, I am not worthy to loose the latchet of his shoe, that is, I do not usurp for myself the name of bridegroom, nor do I wish to be believed or called the bridegroom, but the friend of the bridegroom. For it was the custom that if any man refused to take to wife her who fell to him, the man who should come forward as bridegroom to her by right of kinship would loose his shoe. John therefore, who is not the bridegroom, says: I am not worthy, etc. As if he were to say: I cannot uncover the footsteps of the Redeemer: because I do not usurp for myself the name of bridegroom.

Or he simply humbles himself, or he is not worthy to carry about the sacraments of the Gospel by preaching, which was not assigned to him but committed to the apostles. I am not worthy to unfold the nature of the Divinity to the humanity. Or, I am not worthy to bear the preaching of the Gospel, or to usurp the name of bridegroom. John, as a mere man, could not give the Spirit, by whom guilt is remitted. But Christ gives it, because he is God: and he baptizes in the word, of which it is said: *And you are clean by reason of the word which I have spoken to you ((Joan. XV))* ; and elsewhere: *Cleansing them by the laver of water in the word of sanctified life ((Ephes. V))* .

*In the Holy Spirit.* Either in the spirit of sanctification, and in fire, that is, in the proving of tribulation. Or in the spirit he washes in the present: afterwards, if any stain has crept in, he will burn it away to purity by the fire of purgatory: which is to be believed of the lighter sins. Whence in Leviticus, upon the altar a fire sent down from heaven burned continually, that is, the fire of divine love, which as it were rebaptizes all those in Christ (that is, those who are offered upon the altar) and burns away the vices of their flesh.

*Whose fan.* The fan in his hand is the sifting of judgment by which are distinguished the light and those empty of the fruit of good work. *In his hand,* because the Father judges no man, but has given all judgment to the Son. *He shall thoroughly cleanse,* that is, he daily cleanses from divers temptations. Or, *He shall thoroughly cleanse,* when for manifest sins the perverse man is cast out of the Church, or after death is damned. *But the chaff.* The chaff springs from the same origin as the wheat, that is, from the seed, but the cockle from a different one. The chaff, therefore, are those who are steeped in the sacraments of the faith, but are not solid: the cockle are those who are severed from the elect both in work and in profession. Of these it is said: *He that believeth not is already judged,* and therefore no mention is made here of them. *Unquenchable.* Because it shall not be quenched, neither shall it quench those it torments, but shall punish them eternally. And it is so called by way of distinction from that fire of which it is said: *Thou hast tried us by fire ((Psal. LXV))*, etc.

hymns.title: Wild and lone the prophet's voice
Prepare the way of the Lord

registers.label: Spare
lines: A voice cries out in the wilderness.
Prepare the way of the Lord.
From a cut-down stump, a green shoot rises.
The hope of God is not finished with us.
The wolf will lie down with the lamb.
And a little child will lead them.
Come, let us worship the God who makes peace.
Come, Lord Jesus. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Look at the stump, cut to the ground, and look closer — one green shoot is pushing up through the dead wood.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
Out in the wilderness a rough voice is calling: straighten the road, fill the valleys, make a way home.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
Picture the day the prophet saw — wolf and lamb together, the child unafraid, no one hurt on all God's mountain.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
Welcome one another, then, as Christ has welcomed you, and turn your faces toward the One still coming.
Come, Lord Jesus, come. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: A green shoot breaks from the old dead stump.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
A voice in the wilderness: prepare the way.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
The wolf and the lamb will rest together.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
Come, let us worship the God of peace.
Come, Lord Jesus, come. Amen.
